def: A job category for federal employees whose work influences policy. People in it lose many of the usual protections against being fired, so they can be removed more like political appointees. It was created by a 2020 executive order, cancelled in 2021, and brought back in 2025 under the name "Schedule Policy/Career."
The formal process for laying off federal employees when jobs are cut, usually because of budget cuts or reorganization. It follows set rules about who goes first.
The top tier of career (non-political) managers in federal agencies, just below political appointees.
A federal official picked by the president or the president's team, rather than hired through the regular civil service. They usually leave when an administration ends.
The permanent federal workforce, hired based on merit and protected from being fired for political reasons. They stay from one administration to the next.

A written instruction from the president telling federal agencies how to do their work. It is not a law passed by Congress, a later president can cancel it, and courts can strike it down if it goes beyond the president's legal power.
A formal statement by the president, often used for trade actions like tariffs or for immigration restrictions. Legally it works much like an executive order.
A binding requirement written by a federal agency under power Congress gave it. Agencies usually publish a proposed rule, take public comments, then publish a final rule.
A rule that takes effect right away, before the agency takes public comments. Agencies can use it only in limited situations, such as emergencies.
The usual process for making a rule: the agency publishes its plan, anyone can send comments, and the agency must respond before finalizing it.
Advice an agency publishes about how it reads the law or plans to enforce it. Unlike a rule, guidance is not supposed to be legally binding.
The government's official daily publication of rules, proposed rules, executive orders and notices. If an agency changes a regulation, it shows up here.
A 1946 law that sets the rules agencies must follow when making regulations. Courts can strike down agency actions that are "arbitrary and capricious" or skip required steps.
The legal test courts use to decide whether an agency acted without a reasonable explanation. If so, the court can throw out the action.
A law that lets Congress cancel a recently issued agency rule with a simple majority vote in both chambers and the president's signature.
The laws Congress passes, usually every year, that decide how much money each agency can spend and on what.
When Congress cancels money it already approved but that has not been spent yet. The president can propose rescissions, but Congress has to approve them.

A disputed tactic: the president proposes cancelling money so late in the fiscal year that the funds expire before Congress can vote. Supporters call it legal; critics, including the Government Accountability Office, say it is not.
When a president withholds or delays money Congress approved. A 1974 law, the Impoundment Control Act, limits when this is allowed.
A special budget process that lets some tax and spending bills pass the Senate with a simple majority (51 votes) instead of the usual 60. The 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill Act" passed this way.

The large tax and spending law passed through reconciliation and signed in July 2025. It extended the 2017 tax cuts and changed Medicaid, SNAP, student loans, energy tax credits and immigration enforcement funding.
A lump sum of federal money given to states with broad freedom over how to spend it, instead of money tied to specific program rules.
The federal budget year. It runs from October 1 to September 30, so fiscal year 2026 began on October 1, 2025.
A court order that stops something from happening. A "preliminary" injunction pauses a policy early in a lawsuit, before the final decision; a "permanent" one comes after the court decides the case.
A very short-term court order, often lasting days or weeks, that pauses an action until the court can hold a fuller hearing.
When a court cancels a rule or decision entirely, as if it had never been issued.
When a court sends a matter back to an agency or a lower court to be reconsidered, often without cancelling it.
A court order that pauses something, such as a lower court's ruling, while an appeal goes forward.
When all the active judges of an appeals court hear a case together, instead of the usual panel of three.

A federal appeals court. There are 13; each covers a region (for example, the Ninth Circuit covers western states, and the D.C. Circuit hears many cases about federal agencies). Their rulings can be appealed to the Supreme Court.
The federal trial courts, where most lawsuits start. There are 94 of them.
The Supreme Court's agreement to hear a case. Most requests are turned down.
A lawsuit brought on behalf of a large group of people in a similar situation, so a ruling can protect everyone in the group, not just the named plaintiffs.

A 1935 Supreme Court case that said Congress could protect leaders of some independent agencies from being fired by the president without cause. The Supreme Court overruled it in Trump v. Slaughter (June 2026).
A federal agency, such as the FTC, SEC or FCC, that Congress set up to be somewhat separate from presidential control, usually run by a bipartisan board with fixed terms.

A legal idea that a policy can be discriminatory if it harms one group much more than others, even if no one intended to discriminate. Supporters say it catches hidden bias; critics say it punishes neutral rules.

Short for "diversity, equity, and inclusion": programs and offices meant to recruit, support or train people from different backgrounds. The 2025 executive orders ended most such programs in the federal government.
Part of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 that bans discrimination based on race, color or national origin in programs that get federal money.
Part of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 that bans job discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin.

A 1972 law that bans sex discrimination in schools and colleges that get federal money. It covers sports, harassment and how schools handle complaints. Different administrations have written different rules about what it requires.
The largest federal K-12 program. It sends money (about $18 billion a year) to schools with many students from low-income families.
The Individuals with Disabilities Education Act: the federal law guaranteeing students with disabilities a free public education suited to their needs, with federal money to help pay for it.
Federal college grants for students with financial need. Unlike loans, they do not have to be paid back.
A program that cancels remaining federal student loan debt after 10 years of payments for people working in government or for qualifying nonprofits.
A federal law that protects the privacy of student education records and gives parents rights to see them.
A federal preschool and early-childhood program for children from low-income families.
The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, formerly called food stamps. It helps low-income households buy groceries.
A federal nutrition program for low-income pregnant women, new mothers, babies and young children.
Temporary Assistance for Needy Families: federal cash-assistance money given to states as a block grant.
Health coverage for people with low incomes and some people with disabilities, run by states and paid for jointly by states and the federal government.
Federal health insurance mainly for people 65 and older and some younger people with disabilities.

The 2010 health law, sometimes called Obamacare. It created insurance marketplaces with subsidies, expanded Medicaid in states that opted in, and set rules such as covering people with pre-existing conditions.
Paying doctors and hospitals based on patient results and costs, instead of "fee-for-service," where they are paid for each test, visit or procedure.
A federal program requiring drug makers to sell medicines at a discount to certain hospitals and clinics that serve many low-income patients.
A provision Congress has added to yearly spending laws since 1976 that blocks most federal funding for abortions. Because it is renewed each year, it is not permanent law.
A yearly spending-law provision that bars federal money to governments that discriminate against health providers who refuse to take part in abortions.
The federal family-planning grant program, which funds birth control and related care for low-income people. By law its money cannot pay for abortions.

match: Protecting Life in Global Health Assistance
def: A rule, switched on by Republican presidents and off by Democratic ones since 1984, that bars foreign groups getting U.S. aid from performing or promoting abortion, even with their own money.
A drug approved by the FDA in 2000, used with a second drug to end an early pregnancy. Since 2023 FDA rules have allowed it to be prescribed by telehealth and mailed.
Extra safety rules the FDA can attach to a drug, such as who may prescribe it and how it is dispensed.

An 1873 law that bans mailing items "intended for producing abortion." It has not been enforced that way for decades; a 2022 Justice Department legal opinion said it does not apply to lawful uses of abortion drugs.
The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices: the expert panel that advises the CDC on which vaccines to recommend and when.
The part of the Affordable Care Act that bans discrimination in health programs that get federal money. Administrations have disagreed on whether it covers gender identity.
The President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief: the U.S. global HIV/AIDS program, started in 2003.
Protection the U.S. can give people already here or at the border who show they fear persecution at home because of race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership in a social group.
The program that resettles people screened abroad who are fleeing persecution. The president sets a yearly cap on admissions.
Permission to stay and work in the U.S. for people from countries hit by war or disaster. It lasts only as long as the government keeps renewing it for that country.
Temporary permission to enter or stay in the U.S. for urgent humanitarian reasons or significant public benefit. It is not a visa or legal status.
A fast-track deportation process that skips an immigration judge for certain people who cannot show they have been in the U.S. long enough.
Agreements that let state or local police perform some immigration enforcement tasks for ICE.
An online federal system that lets employers check whether a new hire is allowed to work in the U.S.
A policy that makes some asylum seekers wait in Mexico while their U.S. court cases go forward. Its official name is the Migrant Protection Protocols.
A 1997 court settlement that limits how long and in what conditions the government can detain migrant children.
A state or city that limits how much its police help federal immigration enforcement, for example by not holding people for ICE without a warrant.
A temporary work visa for skilled foreign workers in specialty jobs such as tech or engineering.
Temporary work visas for seasonal foreign workers: H-2A for farm work, H-2B for other seasonal jobs like landscaping or hospitality.
The rule, based on the 14th Amendment, that almost anyone born on U.S. soil is a citizen.
A 1798 law letting the president detain or deport citizens of an enemy nation during a declared war or invasion.
A tax on imported goods, paid by the importer when goods enter the country. Some of the cost is often passed on to buyers.
A 1977 law that lets the president regulate trade and freeze assets during a declared national emergency. In February 2026 the Supreme Court ruled it does not allow tariffs.
Part of a 1962 trade law that lets the president put tariffs on imports that threaten national security, such as steel and aluminum.
Part of a 1974 trade law that lets the U.S. Trade Representative put tariffs on countries found to use unfair trade practices.
Part of a 1974 trade law that allows a temporary tariff of up to 15% for up to 150 days to fix a balance-of-payments problem.
A rule that let packages worth under $800 enter the U.S. without tariffs or most paperwork.
The international body that sets and enforces rules for trade between member countries.
The trade agreement between the U.S., Mexico and Canada that replaced NAFTA in 2020.
The National Environmental Policy Act: a 1970 law requiring federal agencies to study the environmental effects of major projects, like highways or pipelines, before approving them.
The EPA's 2009 conclusion that greenhouse gases endanger public health. It was the legal basis for federal climate rules on cars and power plants until the EPA rescinded it in February 2026.
Short for "waters of the United States": the legal definition of which streams, wetlands and other waters the Clean Water Act protects.
The main federal law controlling air pollution from factories, power plants and vehicles.
The main federal law controlling pollution in rivers, lakes and wetlands.
A 1973 law protecting plants and animals at risk of extinction and the habitats they depend on.
A 1906 law that lets the president protect federal land as a national monument without a vote of Congress.
A family of long-lasting man-made chemicals, sometimes called "forever chemicals," used in nonstick and water-resistant products and linked to health problems.
The federal program for cleaning up the most contaminated hazardous-waste sites.
A Biden-era goal to conserve 30% of U.S. land and water by 2030. It was revoked in 2025.
Corporate Average Fuel Economy standards: federal rules setting how many miles per gallon carmakers' vehicles must average.
Permission from the EPA that lets California set its own, stricter vehicle-pollution rules, which other states can then copy.
Liquefied natural gas: natural gas cooled into a liquid so it can be shipped overseas by tanker.
Short for "environmental, social, and governance": factors some investors weigh, such as climate risk or labor practices, beyond pure financial return.
The federal law setting standards for private retirement and health plans offered by employers.
A 1931 law requiring contractors on federal construction projects to pay workers the local "prevailing wage."
A pre-hire deal for a construction project that sets wages and work rules, usually negotiated with unions.
A 1920 law requiring ships that carry goods between U.S. ports to be U.S.-built, U.S.-owned and mostly U.S.-crewed.
A 1996 law that protects websites and apps from most lawsuits over what their users post, and over their good-faith decisions to remove content.

Part of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act that lets intelligence agencies collect communications of foreigners abroad without a warrant, which can sweep in Americans' messages with them. Congress must periodically renew it.
A law that lets the president use the military inside the U.S. to put down rebellions or enforce the law in extreme situations.
Military reserve forces controlled by each state's governor, which the president can call into federal service in some situations.
A digital form of a country's money issued directly by its central bank, here the Federal Reserve.
Government-backed companies that buy home mortgages from lenders, making more money available for home loans. They have been under federal control since the 2008 financial crisis.
The Federal Reserve's two goals set by Congress: stable prices and maximum employment.
A 2021 law requiring many small companies to report their real owners to the Treasury, to fight money laundering.
The U.S. Agency for International Development, which ran most U.S. foreign aid until it was largely shut down and folded into the State Department in 2025.
The U.S. Agency for Global Media, which runs government-funded international news outlets such as Voice of America.

The private nonprofit Congress created in 1967 to pass federal money to public TV and radio stations, including those carrying PBS and NPR programs. Congress cancelled its funding in 2025, and its board voted to dissolve in January 2026.
The Office of Personnel Management: the federal government's human-resources agency, which sets hiring, pay and firing rules for most civilian employees.
The Office of Management and Budget, part of the White House. It writes the president's budget, oversees how agencies spend money, and reviews major regulations.

match: Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs
def: The office inside OMB that reviews major regulations before agencies issue them.
The White House office that finds and vets people for the president to appoint to political jobs across the government.
The Government Accountability Office: Congress's nonpartisan watchdog that audits federal agencies and spending.
The Congressional Research Service: nonpartisan researchers who write background reports for members of Congress.
The Department of Homeland Security, which includes immigration agencies (ICE, CBP, USCIS), FEMA, TSA and the Coast Guard.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement: the DHS agency that arrests, detains and deports people inside the U.S. who are in violation of immigration law.
Customs and Border Protection, which runs border crossings and the Border Patrol and collects tariffs.
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which handles applications for visas, green cards, citizenship and asylum.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency, which coordinates disaster response and aid.
The Transportation Security Administration, which screens passengers and bags at airports.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which protects government networks and critical systems like power grids and election equipment.

match: Department of Health and Human Services
def: The Department of Health and Human Services, which includes the FDA, CDC, NIH and CMS.

match: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services
def: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, which runs Medicare, Medicaid and the ACA marketplaces.
The Food and Drug Administration, which approves drugs and medical devices and regulates food safety.

match: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
def: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the federal public-health agency that tracks diseases and issues health guidance.
The National Institutes of Health, the main federal funder of medical research.
The Environmental Protection Agency, which writes and enforces rules on air, water and chemical pollution.
The Department of Energy, which runs national labs, the nuclear weapons program, energy research and loan programs.
The National Nuclear Security Administration, part of DOE, which maintains the U.S. nuclear weapons stockpile.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, which regulates interstate electricity, gas pipelines and the power grid.
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission, which licenses and oversees nuclear power plants.
The Department of Justice, the federal government's law office. It prosecutes federal crimes, represents the government in court and includes the FBI.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Justice Department's main investigative and domestic-intelligence agency.
The Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel, which writes legal opinions that the executive branch treats as binding.
The Department of Defense (renamed the Department of War by executive order in 2025), which runs the military.

match: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
def: The Office of the Director of National Intelligence, which oversees the 18 U.S. intelligence agencies, including the CIA and NSA.
The National Security Council: the president's main group of advisers on foreign policy and defense.
The Department of Agriculture, which runs farm programs, food safety inspection, the Forest Service and nutrition programs such as SNAP.

match: Department of Housing and Urban Development
def: The Department of Housing and Urban Development, which runs public housing, rental assistance and fair-housing enforcement.
The Department of Labor, which enforces wage, workplace-safety and retirement-plan laws.
The Occupational Safety and Health Administration, which sets and enforces workplace-safety rules.
The National Labor Relations Board, which oversees union elections and private-sector labor disputes.
The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, which enforces laws against job discrimination.
The Department of Transportation, which oversees highways, aviation (through the FAA), railroads and transit.
The Federal Aviation Administration, which runs air traffic control and regulates aviation safety.
The Department of Veterans Affairs, which runs veterans' health care, disability benefits and cemeteries.
The Internal Revenue Service, which collects federal taxes.
The Securities and Exchange Commission, which regulates the stock market and companies that sell stock to the public.
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, created in 2010 to oversee banks and lenders on things like mortgages, credit cards and debt collection.
The Federal Trade Commission, which enforces consumer-protection and antitrust (competition) laws.
The Federal Communications Commission, which regulates broadcasting, phone and internet services.
The Federal Election Commission, which enforces campaign-finance laws. It has six commissioners, no more than three from one party.
The Small Business Administration, which backs small-business loans and runs contracting programs for small firms.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, which negotiates trade deals and enforces trade laws such as Section 301.
The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, which controls exports of sensitive technology.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which includes the National Weather Service and ocean and climate research.
The Bureau of Land Management, which manages about 245 million acres of federal land, mostly in the West, including oil, gas and grazing leases.
The White House Council on Environmental Quality, which coordinates environmental policy and NEPA guidance.

match: Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States
def: The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, which reviews foreign purchases of U.S. companies for national-security risks.
The North Atlantic Treaty Organization: the military alliance of the U.S., Canada and European countries, which promise to defend each other.
The United Nations agency for international public health. The U.S. withdrew from it in January 2026.
The 2015 international climate agreement in which countries set their own targets to cut greenhouse-gas emissions.
